title: Chapter III

teacherSummary.text: Victor's mother dies of scarlet fever caught while nursing Elizabeth, and on her deathbed asks Victor and Elizabeth to marry. Victor leaves for the University of Ingolstadt, where M. Krempe scorns his alchemists and M. Waldman inspires him with modern chemistry.

vocabulary.definition: To preoccupy, as ground or land
vocabulary.context: Krempe was a little squat man, with a gruff voice and a repulsive countenance; the teacher, therefore, did not prepossess me in favour of his pursuits.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “prepossess”: pre- (Latin prae, "before") + pos (Latin ponere, "to place"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A vessel or melting pot, composed of some very refractory substance, as clay, graphite, platinum, and used for…
vocabulary.context: But these philosophers, whose hands seem only made to dabble in dirt, and their eyes to pore over the microscope or crucible, have indeed performed miracles.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “crucible”: -ible (Latin -ibilis, "able to be"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Dwelling, or having an abode, in a place for a continued length of time
vocabulary.context: Such were my reflections during the first two or three days of my residence at Ingolstadt, which were chiefly spent in becoming acquainted with the localities, and the principal residents in my new abode.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “resident”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Weariness from bodily labor or mental exertion
vocabulary.context: I had sufficient leisure for these and many other reflections during my journey to Ingolstadt, which was long and fatiguing.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “fatigue”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: (Myth.) A monster represented as vomiting flames, and as having the head of a lion, the body of a goat, and the tail…
vocabulary.context: I was required to exchange chimeras of boundless grandeur for realities of little worth.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “chimera”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To change from one nature, form, or substance, into another
vocabulary.context: The modern masters promise very little; they know that metals cannot be transmuted, and that the elixir of life is a chimera.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “transmute”: trans- (Latin trans, "across"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: An oration or eulogy in praise of some person or achievement
vocabulary.context: After having made a few preparatory experiments, he concluded with a panegyric upon modern chemistry, the terms of which I shall never forget:—
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “panegyric”: -ic (Greek -ikos, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A rising against civil or political authority, or the established government
vocabulary.context: My internal being was in a state of insurrection and turmoil; I felt that order would thence arise, but I had no power to produce it.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “insurrection”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To have a beginning or origin
vocabulary.context: These are the reflections of the first days; but when the lapse of time proves the reality of the evil, then the actual bitterness of grief commences.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “commence”: com- (Latin com-, "with, together"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Good God! in what desert land have you lived, where no one was kind enough to inform you that these fancies, which you have so greedily imbibed, are a thousand years old, and as musty as they are ancient?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “imbibe”: im- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Ingolstadt (Bavaria) had a real university and was associated with the Illuminati, a secret society. Chemistry was rapidly changing in this era.

significance: Grief and ambition merge; Waldman's speech about scientists who 'penetrate into the recesses of nature' ignites Victor's resolve.
discussionQuestions: How might his mother's death affect Victor's desire to conquer death?
Where does foreshadowing appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with nature versus nurture?

items.prompt: Where does Victor go to university?
How does M. Krempe react to Victor's reading?
options: He scorns it as outdated nonsense
He gives Victor more alchemy books

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter III,” how does Shelley show loss and leaving home? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter III, how does Shelley develop the idea of loss and leaving home? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the foreshadowing in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter III develops the idea of loss and leaving home. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter III (where it begins, turns and ends) and its foreshadowing shape the reader's understanding of loss and leaving home. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter III suggests about loss and leaving home. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's foreshadowing and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses foreshadowing in Chapter III to complicate the reader's understanding of loss and leaving home. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter III within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of loss and leaving home responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter III alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of loss and leaving home follows or bends those conventions, using the foreshadowing as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter III and its treatment of loss and leaving home. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's foreshadowing and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter III as evidence for a larger claim about loss and leaving home in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter III as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of loss and leaving home. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.passage: Such were my reflections during the first two or three days of my residence at Ingolstadt, which were chiefly spent in becoming acquainted with the localities, and the principal residents in my new abode.
satQuestions.prompt: As used in the text, what does the word “residents” most nearly mean?
options: A rising against civil or political authority, or the established government
Dwelling, or having an abode, in a place for a continued length of time

satQuestions.passage: I had sufficient leisure for these and many other reflections during my journey to Ingolstadt, which was long and fatiguing. At length the high white steeple of the town met my eyes. I alighted, and was conducted to my solitary apartment, to spend the evening as I pleased.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter III”?
options: The pain of a father's love

annotationFocus.label: Foreshadowing
annotationFocus.lookFor: hints, warnings or images that point to later events
annotationFocus.passage: I had sufficient leisure for these and many other reflections during my journey to Ingolstadt, which was long and fatiguing. At length the high white steeple of the town met my eyes. I alighted, and was conducted to my solitary apartment, to spend the evening as I pleased.

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them

annotationFocus.label: Tone / mood
annotationFocus.lookFor: word choices that reveal the narrator's attitude or the scene's feeling

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: How might his mother's death affect Victor's desire to conquer death? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are prepossess, crucible, residents, fatiguing, chimeras. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Krempe was a little squat man, with a gruff voice and a repulsive countenance; the teacher, therefore, did not prepossess me in favour of his pursuits.” Webster's says: To preoccupy, as ground or land. Now the word history: “prepossess”: pre- (Latin prae, "before") + pos (Latin ponere, "to place"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “crucible”: -ible (Latin -ibilis, "able to be"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “resident”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Ingolstadt (Bavaria) had a real university and was associated with the Illuminati, a secret society. Chemistry was rapidly changing in this era. Why does this chapter matter? Grief and ambition merge; Waldman's speech about scientists who 'penetrate into the recesses of nature' ignites Victor's resolve. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for foreshadowing.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see foreshadowing, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to loss and leaving home.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Foreshadowing, Characterization, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of foreshadowing. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: I had sufficient leisure for these and many other reflections during my journey to Ingolstadt, which was long and fatiguing. At length the high white steeple of the town met my eyes. I alighted, and was conducted to my solitary apartment, to spend the evening as I pleased.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Foreshadowing, Characterization, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter III,” how does Shelley show loss and leaving home? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about loss and leaving home, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how foreshadowing shapes loss and leaving home. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
